summary: Apertura is a free web telescope over the real infrared sky of NASA's SPHEREx mission. Drag to turn it, scroll to zoom, step through its near-infrared channels from 0.75 to 5 µm, or search any object by name or coordinates, in English or Ukrainian. One button pulls every SPHEREx exposure of that spot from NASA's IRSA archive, aligns them and plays them as a time-lapse. A difference mode hides the stars that stay put, so whatever moved or changed brightness stands out. The result can be shared as a short video. SPHEREx data is open, but it sits in 65 MB FITS files behind archive queries that mostly specialists use. Apertura reads only the pixels it needs, about 36 KB per frame, and puts them in front of anyone with a browser or a phone, with no install and no account. That is the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge: type the RA and Dec of any patch of sky, or open a link with them in the URL, and Apertura plays every SPHEREx image of it as a little video, so a point of light that shifts between dates, the way Pluto did, is easy to spot.
details:
Apertura turns NASA's SPHEREx survey into a telescope anyone can use. The landing page is the instrument: a dial with an eyepiece showing the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky map, with the coordinates you are pointing at (RA, Dec, field of view) underneath. You turn it by dragging, zoom with the wheel, change the wavelength with a slider, adjust brightness and contrast, switch between false colour and the original greyscale, and open the sky full screen. A catalogue of 20 starting points (galaxies, nebulae, stars, clusters, infrared sources) and a search box that understands object names in English and Ukrainian, catalogue designations and coordinates take you anywhere on the sky.

The main feature is the time-lapse. For the spot you are looking at, Apertura finds every SPHEREx exposure in the archive, cuts the same 6-arcminute patch out of each one, aligns them north up on a common grid and plays them in date order, one detector at a time. Stars stay still; things that move or vary do not. Difference mode subtracts the first frame so those changes stand out. The sequence is rendered in the browser into a 1080x1350 MP4 card with the date, coordinates and detector, ready to post, together with a link that reopens the same observation.

How it uses NASA data

1. The eyepiece shows the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky data cube that NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) publishes in HiPS format, one sky per spectral channel. It is drawn with Aladin Lite. Tiles pass through our own caching proxy, because loading them straight from IRSA under load dropped connections.

2. For a time-lapse we query IRSA's Simple Image Access (SIA v2) service for the spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3 collections and get every exposure that covers the position, with its detector and observation time.

3. Each exposure is a 65 MB FITS file. Our serverless function reads it from IRSA's public AWS S3 bucket with two HTTP range requests: the header, then only the detector rows that cross the patch (about 0.8 MB). It resamples the patch north up onto a fixed grid, subtracts the background and sends about 36 KB to the browser. If the bucket is unreachable it falls back to IRSA's cutout service.

4. Object names are resolved through CDS Sesame (SIMBAD) and NASA/IPAC's NED, plus a bundled Ukrainian dictionary built from Wikidata.

Tools and languages

JavaScript (ES modules, no framework) in the browser; Node.js serverless functions on Vercel; Aladin Lite (WebGL and WebAssembly) for the sky; our own FITS reader and resampling for the cutouts; Canvas, WebCodecs and mp4-muxer for the video, with MediaRecorder as a fallback; Python for building the Ukrainian name dictionary. No database, no accounts, no tracking.

What we considered

Speed and cost: reading 36 KB instead of 65 MB per frame makes a time-lapse take seconds and keeps the serverless functions cheap. We also profiled the page and removed everything that kept the browser busy while idle.

Reliability: the archive can be slow or down, so tile requests are retried and cached, cutouts have a fallback source, and every failure shows a plain message instead of a broken view.

Honesty about the data: false colour is labelled as such and the original greyscale is one click away. Frames are compared only within one detector, and the page explains why brightness can wander between dates while positions do not.

Access: free, nothing to install, works on phones, full Ukrainian and English interface, labelled controls for screen readers, and reduced motion settings are respected.

How it meets the challenge

Enter coordinates: the search box takes RA and Dec in decimal degrees or sexagesimal (for example 08h55m10.831s -7d14m42.53s for WISE 0855), as well as object names.

Show the patch as a little video: every SPHEREx exposure of that position is cut to the same patch, aligned north up and played in date order, with play/pause and a clickable timeline of dates.

Make motion easy to spot: difference mode subtracts the first frame from each later one, so fixed stars cancel and anything that moved or changed brightness remains.

Test targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis can all be reached from the search box by name or coordinates.

Easy to update with new data: the archive collections are a one-line list (currently spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3) and frames are fetched live from IRSA, so new releases appear without changes to the site.

The 102 bands: the all-sky map lets you step through the channels with a slider, and time-lapses are built per detector array (D1 to D6), so you compare like with like.

Coordinates in the URL: every observation has a link (?ra=&dec=&fov=&name=) that reopens it, so it can be embedded or shared.

Aladin Lite from CDS draws the sky, as the challenge suggests.

What is creative about it

Most ways into survey data start with a query form. Apertura starts with an instrument: the setting circle turns as you pan, an iris closes while the telescope slews and opens when the new sky has arrived, and the eyepiece rim flashes when you take a time-lapse. The time dimension of an all-sky survey, invisible on a static map, becomes something you can watch and share.

Intended impact

People who would never open a FITS file get to point a NASA space telescope themselves and see that the sky changes. Teachers get a free classroom tool in Ukrainian and English. Every shared clip links back to its observation, so each post invites someone else to look.

What we would build next

Stacking all frames of one detector to raise signal-to-noise, and adding as well as subtracting images from different dates.

Spectra on the fly from the 102 bands for a clicked source.

A user-chosen field of view for time-lapses (it is fixed at 6 arcminutes now, which keeps each frame small and fast).

Gaia and WISE catalogue overlays through Aladin Lite, and display of SPHEREx quality and contamination flags.

Proper-motion correction, so fast stars searched by name are centred at their current position rather than their catalogue epoch.
